finding.claim: The /invoice/<inv_id> route returns any invoice with no authentication or ownership check (IDOR / broken access control). The sibling route /my/invoice/<inv_id> enforces inv['customer'] == g.user['id'], which shows the check is intended and missing here. Any caller who knows or guesses an invoice ID can read another customer's invoice.
finding.source: Attacker-controlled URL path parameter inv_id on an unauthenticated or any-authenticated request to GET /invoice/<inv_id>
finding.sink: jsonify(inv) returns the full invoice record (including the customer field and other data) from the INVOICES store

trace.note: Route /invoice/<inv_id> is registered with no auth decorator and no before_request hook in the file
INVOICES.get(inv_id) fetches the record by the user-supplied key with no ownership comparison
The full invoice is serialized and returned to the caller

finding.guards_checked: Searched the only file in the directory for before_request, login decorators, and a comparison of inv['customer'] against g.user. None are on this route. The /my/* routes at lines 16 and 23 do compare against g.user, but this route does not. No global auth middleware exists in the codebase. If one is defined elsewhere, it would only authenticate the caller and would still not enforce per-invoice ownership.

verdict.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers /invoice/<inv_id> with no auth decorator or before_request, fetches INVOICES.get(inv_id) and returns it with no ownership check, unlike /my/invoice at line 16.

verdict_facts.reason: invoices.py:7-10 registers /invoice/<inv_id> with no decorator or check, fetches INVOICES.get(inv_id) and returns jsonify(inv), whereas the sibling route at invoices.py:16 does enforce inv["customer"] != g.user["id"], so any client who supplies an invoice ID can read another customer's invoice.
